title: Better speech synthesis for audiobooks
abstract: Text-to-speech systems — which convert written text into synthetic speech — display impressive naturalness in applications such as chatbots and virtual assistants, where interactions last seconds. But they tend not to fare as well with longer-form content. When applied to audiobooks, for instance, conventional text-to-speech (TTS) models fail to reliably change speaking style between characters, as a human narrator would. This creates two problems for listeners: (1) distinguishing narration from dialogue and (2) identifying which character speaks which lines. To address this problem, the Audible technology team is using controllable TTS, meaning the ability to control dialogue delivery with natural-language speech descriptions (e.g., "speak in an enthusiastic, high-pitched voice"). This allows the TTS model to leverage the deep textual understanding of large language models (LLMs) to synthesize high-quality speech. Our approach involves three key innovations. First, we developed a novel data synthesis pipeline to produce speech data captioned with high-quality descriptions of speech characteristics. Training on this data enables our model to understand captions and produce audio consistent with them at inference time. Second, we created a system that automatically profiles characters in books and identifies their dialogue with 97% accuracy. It also provides captions for that dialogue, which act as stage directions for the model. Third, we used the first two techniques to synthesize audiobooks featuring distinct character voices, improving dialogue differentiation by 3.7 points on a MUSHRA (multiple stimuli with hidden reference and anchor) test, a standardized method where listeners rate audio quality on a scale from 0 to 100. Across tests in both English and Spanish, we observe statistically significant improvement in listening experience for eight out of ten voices. TTS for audiobooks Subtle defects in synthetic speech, such as unnatural prosody or monotone delivery, are tolerable for short stretches but become increasingly grating over time — and audiobook listeners engage with the same voice for 10 to 15 hours per book. This is why off-the-shelf TTS models often fail to produce enjoyable, natural audiobook narrations. Furthermore, general-purpose TTS models are designed to process individual utterances with minimal context. That’s a reasonable approach when responding to questions like "What's the weather today?", but it’s inadequate for audiobooks, where narrative coherence depends on understanding the surrounding story context. A TTS model reading dialogue needs to know whether the speaker is the protagonist confronting an antagonist or a minor character making small talk, information that may only be available in earlier chapters. Finally, general-purpose models struggle to produce character voices in a consistent and natural way across the span of an entire book, often voicing a character in a markedly different way in chapter 1 than in chapter 10. Controllable text-to-speech I. The data synthesis pipeline Whereas conventional TTS models are trained on text-speech pairs, a controllable-TTS model also requires annotations that describe how the speech sounds. The speech in the training set also needs to be highly expressive, covering the wide variety of dimensions — pitch, speaking rate, character voices, emotions, speaking styles, etc. — the model must control. Previous TTS models couldn't handle that kind of expressivity, so most existing training data is neutral in tone. We expanded the training sets through two approaches: new recordings and human captioning of existing audio data. While there are some datasets that include descriptions of prosodic features, each has its own description format: some are long, some are short, and some use single tags. title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
abstract: Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome. Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder . The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result. This post uses Wordle , a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting. In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models . All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository . Solution overview The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect. Figure 1: MTRL on SageMaker AI, where the training job invokes the AgentCore-hosted agent once per rollout to sample the policy model, play the game, and report a reward For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word , and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ) adapter on the policy model. Three design points matter for what follows: The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function. The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring. The reward is outcome-dominant. A solve pays 1.05–1.55 depending on speed, a loss pays -0.5

title: Orchestrating SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling with AWS CDK
abstract: Updating the Amazon Sagemaker AI real-time endpoint configuration (changing the instance type, instance count, or environment variables) causes deployments through AWS CloudFormation or the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to fail. SageMaker AI requires you to deregister the scalable target before updating the endpoint, but when you deregister it, CloudFormation can’t track the AWS Application Auto Scaling resources. In this post, we show you how to use a reusable CDK construct with AWS CloudFormation custom resources to orchestrate deregister and register auto scaling automatically during endpoint updates. You can update your endpoint configuration and auto scaling parameters in a single deployment without manual intervention. Why this problem occurs When you deploy a SageMaker AI endpoint with native CloudFormation auto scaling resources, then change the endpoint configuration and redeploy, several failure modes emerge. The specific failure depends on what you change and how you work around the issue. Changing the endpoint configuration with auto scaling registered CloudFormation tries to update the endpoint while the scalable target is still registered. SageMaker AI rejects the update with the following error: The variant(s) "[AllTraffic]" must be deregistered as scalable targets with Application Auto Scaling before they can be removed or have their instance type updated. SageMaker AI blocks the endpoint update before CloudFormation reaches the auto scaling resources. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing only the endpoint configuration If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and redeploy with only an endpoint configuration change, the deployment succeeds. However, CloudFormation doesn’t register auto scaling even though it is in the CloudFormation template. Because the auto scaling parameters in the CloudFormation template haven’t changed, CloudFormation doesn’t register the scalable target or re-apply the scaling policy. The endpoint is now running without auto scaling, and there is no error to indicate anything went wrong. Manually deregistering auto scaling, then changing auto scaling parameters If you deregister the scalable target through the AWS CLI and redeploy with auto scaling parameter changes, CloudFormation tries to update the ScalableTarget resource that no longer exists: Resource of type 'AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget' with identifier 'endpoint/<name>/variant/AllTraffic|sagemaker:variant:DesiredInstanceCount|sagemaker' was not found. This failure is notable because the rollback also fails (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED), leaving the stack in a broken state that requires manual intervention in the CloudFormation console to recover. Solution overview You can use this CDK construct to replace the native AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget and AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalingPolicy CloudFormation resources with three custom resources. These custom resources deregister and register auto scaling around the endpoint update with explicit dependency ordering, enforced by node.add_dependency calls in CDK. The full sequence is: Deregister (custom resource): Removes the scalable target before the endpoint update begins. On first deploy, no scalable target exists yet, so the handler handles the error gracefully and continues. Endpoint update (CDK-managed): CDK updates the endpoint resource normally, swapping to the new endpoint configuration. Register Scalable Target (custom resource): Waits for the endpoint to reach InService status, then registers the scalable target. Attach Scaling Policy (custom resource): Waits for the scalable target to be queryable, then applies the target tracking policy. title: Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps
abstract: With Amazon Quick Sight layer maps, you can now plot points and routes, like store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport. Geospatial maps help businesses spot patterns that are tied to location, like how a region is performing or where customers are concentrated. Amazon Quick Sight supports this with multiple map types, including point maps, filled maps, and layer maps. When layer maps first launched , you could upload a GeoJSON file to draw custom shape layers, such as sales territories or districts, and join those shapes to a dataset. That handled regions and boundaries well, but it didn’t cover the individual locations inside them or the routes running between them. Layer maps now support two more geometry types from the same GeoJSON workflow: Point and LineString . Points mark specific locations, such as individual store or facility sites. A LineString traces the route between locations, like a delivery path or a flight between airports. Amazon Quick Sight , the business intelligence (BI) capability of Amazon Quick , is a unified BI service. It delivers modern interactive dashboards, natural language querying, pixel-perfect reports, machine learning (ML) insights, and embedded analytics at scale. Amazon Quick brings together AI agents for business insights, research, and automation in one integrated experience, helping you work smarter and faster while maintaining security and access policies. In this post, we walk through the dataset and GeoJSON structure that layer maps require. We also explain how points and lines work in a layer map visual and when to choose each. Finally, we cover advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering geometries, and updating GeoJSON files programmatically. Dataset structure considerations A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a Quick Sight dataset, and a shared key joins the two. How you structure each one determines what the map can show. This section covers what you need before you start and how a GeoJSON file is organized. Prerequisites The following are the prerequisites that you need before creating a layer map in Quick Sight: A GeoJSON file describing your geometry. A Quick Sight dataset holding the metrics and dimensions. A join key shared between the Quick Sight dataset and the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON file must be saved in .geojson format, with a maximum supported file size of 100 MB. Structure of the GeoJSON file GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for describing geographic features such as points and lines. { "type": "FeatureCollection", "features": [{ "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "Point", "coordinates": [88.4, 22.6] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }, { "type": "Feature", "geometry": { "type": "LineString", "coordinates": [ [88.2, 22.4], [88.9, 23.1], [89.5, 22.8], [90.1, 23.6] ] }, "properties": { "prop0": "value0" } }] } The structure of the file is as follows: FeatureCollection is the whole file. It has a type of FeatureCollection and a features array. Feature is a single map element. It carries a geometry (the shape) and a properties object, which holds the join key. geometry has a type (Point, LineString, or Polygon) and its coordinates . The coordinates hold a single [longitude, latitude] position for a Point , and an ordered list of positions for a LineString . title: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations
abstract: Plant breeding decisions depend on data that spans genomics, field trials, imagery, environmental conditions, and model outputs. Bayer Crop Science runs hundreds of machine learning (ML) model configurations against this data across crops, regions, and teams, and each run needs to be repeatable and governed. To meet that requirement, Bayer built the Connected Decision Engine (CDE), a system for deploying, orchestrating, monitoring, and reusing ML workflows. CDE gives breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and data engineers a consistent way to run analytics while preserving execution history and operational controls. As adoption grew, the bottleneck moved from running workflows to understanding them. Explaining a result meant piecing together context from APIs, documentation, metadata stores, dashboards, and logs. A user who wanted to know why a workflow failed, what a model did, or where a result came from still had to know which system to inspect. To close that gap, Bayer built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent, natural language interface over CDE. A supervisor agent routes each question to a specialist agent, the specialist retrieves context from the relevant system, and the user receives an answer without navigating the operational stack. In its first phase, ADE resolves about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop. ADE runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , an AWS service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore let the team focus on agent behavior instead of building and operating its own agent hosting, session isolation, and tool access layer. Three AgentCore capabilities drove that choice: a managed runtime that isolates each user session, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped tool access through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, that keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code, and a framework-agnostic design that let the team bring its own LangGraph orchestration and choice of models. To prepare for launch and to operate ADE afterward, Bayer engaged AWS Unified Operations . The engagement provided a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and a generative AI Domain Specialist Engineer (DSE), who worked as an extension of the ADE team from design through production. The TAM, as Bayer’s strategic advisor, brought an established understanding of Bayer’s operating model and business priorities. The DSE brought generative AI domain expertise on AWS. In three technical standups each week, the team reviewed and made design decisions. The DSE built working knowledge of the ADE workload and how the Bayer team operates, so technical guidance reflected both AWS service behavior and Bayer’s context. This post follows that journey: the ADE architecture, five design decisions made during the build, the work to prepare the platform for production, and how it is operated after launch. Architecture overview ADE is organized into four layers: the user experience, agent orchestration, specialist agents, and the tools and data sources those agents call (Figure 1). Users reach ADE through a React web front end, and requests pass through an identity proxy for Microsoft Entra ID before they reach the agents. GitHub Actions builds the agent container images, pushes them to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) , and deploys them to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the agents, and because the runtime is framework-agnostic, the team runs its own LangGraph-based orchestration on it directly. The team chose LangGraph for its explicit graph-based control flow and checkpointing for multi-step workflows. LangGraph orchestrates the workflow, with a Supervisor Agent as the entry point that classifies each request, selects a specialist, and combines results when a question spans domains. The data plane is separated by responsibility.

title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
abstract: By Roberto Perez Alcolea , Java Platform Team Quasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decision At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed. The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it. Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves. Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next: Does any consumer still call this method? Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations? Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact? Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign? At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds. Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally. We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions: What changed in the library’s public API? Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed? The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing. From API Changes to Consumer Impact Existing techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive. Quasar builds on SCIP , an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently. On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change. During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings

Owners, Not Renters: Raffi Krikorian on Open Source AI
abstract: Created by Claude with light editing by Tim O’Reilly Raffi Krikorian, Mozilla’s CTO, joined Tim O’Reilly at our recent AI Codecon to talk about open source AI. Mozilla, of course, is the nonprofit that helped to define the open source revolution back in the late 1990s. Though its Firefox web browser was superseded as the market leader by Google Chrome, it played an essential role, along with Apache and the World Wide Web Consortium, in establishing the open standards of the web and keeping it from being dominated and enclosed by Microsoft, the dominant tech platform of that time. Now, Mozilla is one of the leading voices working to build an open, standards-based AI ecosystem. Tim has long appreciated Raffi’s thoughtful, human-centered approach to technology. Raffi writes a newsletter called Owners Not Renters , whose message can be summed up by his statement that he doesn’t want a future with seven AGIs. He wants one with seven billion. He wants each of us to have an AI that we can trust with our secrets and that will look out for our interests, not an AI that’s optimized for the business model of its creators. In the early days of the web, we called the browser a user agent for a reason, Raffi said. It was on your side. It let you render pages however you wanted, managed your privacy and your cookies, and did its best to protect you from those who wanted to take advantage of web users. We need the same thing in the age of AI. Raffi cited a paper in which researchers tested whether AI assistants could be trained to favor a company’s commercial interests over user welfare. In simulated flight-booking requests, 18 of 23 models recommended a more expensive sponsored option over a cheaper one more than half the time. It’s a hypothetical choice that we’ve seen play out time and time again, in industry after industry. Open source AI is a big part of what it will take to get to Raffi’s vision. But sovereign AI loyal to each individual needs more than open source models alone. Raffi’s list of what has to be built around the model starts with memory, a place where your private data can live. It includes tool calling, so an agent can make a purchase or book a doctor’s appointment for you, the runtime environment where all of that runs, and the rules for how his agent talks to those working on behalf of others. It needs a harness. “That’s where evaluations happen. Guardrails happen, execution loops happen, tool calling happens, memory,” he explained. “All of that stuff is an opportunity, in my mind, of things that open source developers can be building.” People hear the word “harness” and conclude that we need an open source version of whatever the proprietary labs are building. Tim asked Raffi whether a user-centered harness might do different things than those offered by the big labs. He agreed. The whole point of open source is for people to “scratch their own itch.” The ability to innovate without permission is the heart of the open source promise. As a result, Mozilla wants to build a starting point. It aims to help the community define what an open memory protocol, a storage protocol, or authenticated tool calling with the right guardrails ought to look like. As Raffi noted, “Once we could define what those open standards look like, then a whole plethora of people can start playing and be interoperable. It’s basically. . .the internet all over again. We can build trillions of dollars of market cap on top of open protocols.” Ease of use is still lacking, though. Mozilla’s 2026 State of Open Source AI report says open models are now within about 3% of the frontier, yet they don’t make it into production at the same rate as closed models. When Tim asked why, Raffi explained that open source is easy to release but hard to deploy. Developers still have to figure out hosting, provisioning, guardrails, and memory. title: The Agentic Software Factory Hierarchy of Needs
abstract: The following article originally appeared on the Vanishing Gradients Substack and is being republished here with the authors’ permission. Stripe’s Minions turn engineering requests into candidate pull requests. Ramp’s Inspect puts coding agents to work in the background, with tools to check their changes. Warp Factories takes work from tickets and chat through agents, checks, and human review. Agentic software factories are here. Are you sick and tired of babysitting Codex, Claude Code, or OpenClaw? Do you have agents that can build features, but still leave you responsible for remembering where they stopped, explaining how each feature fits the project and deciding what happens next? You make progress in each conversation, then development waits for you to return. It doesn’t have to be this way. A software factory lets you delegate more of that process! You agree on an outcome, give the system the context and authority it needs, and let it work while you do something else. When you return, there should be a result you can inspect, with evidence of what was checked, or a specific reason the work could not continue. Your next conversation can then focus on the result and the decisions that remain. As we’ll show you, your first software factory doesn’t need to be that complex at all: It can begin with a single agent and an automation. What makes it a factory The defining combination is autonomous and asynchronous execution . Autonomous: The agent chooses and carries out steps towards an agreed goal. It can inspect what happened, adjust its approach and continue within its authority. Asynchronous: That work can proceed without your ongoing attention. You can leave and return to its result. A scheduled job can run without you. A coding agent can choose and revise an approach during an interactive session. A factory combines those capabilities, with enough context, tools and feedback to carry out the delegated work. Software factories have been hypothesized for decades. Now that we have agents, we’re actually able to operate them. The principles apply to software work traditionally carried out by teams of humans, from bespoke tools for teams and individuals to large and complex software systems. To illustrate these principles, we’ll use an invoice tracker throughout this article, an application we’ve needed for our own businesses. The same approach applies to research tools, publishing systems, and software for teams. Suppose you run a small business and want an invoice tracker that fits how you work. Build an app that creates invoices from my template and tracks which are unpaid, paid, or overdue. Keep it local for now. Preserve the records when it restarts, and show me checks that the totals and payment statuses are correct. You can agree on this brief with the agent, leave it to work while you do something else, and return to the app and evidence of what was checked. If a check fails, it can investigate and adjust within its agreed scope. If it encounters a product decision it cannot make, it should bring that question back to you. You might imagine a clean separation: The factory builds the invoice tracker, then the finished app does its job. That’s one way to run it. But agents can also help operate the software they build, and that combination is useful. The tracker can store invoices and calculate outstanding balances. An agent can use those records alongside customer correspondence to prepare follow-ups: One customer has promised to pay on Friday; another is disputing a charge. You don’t need to turn every situation into a new software feature before the agent can help. You give it the relevant context, authority, and a way to check its work. title: Building Reasoning Models from the Ground Up: A Full Video Course
abstract: I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. Scope and prerequisites The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
abstract: Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes. I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood , and the Hulu series The Dropout , starring Amanda Seyfried. Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything . In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood. Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old. Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015 . Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong. In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023. It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film. As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer , there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her? I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie? But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune ’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT ’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022 . title: A 1,000-mile cloud on Mars may reveal physics never seen in nature
abstract: Every morning during the Martian spring and summer, a thin and extremely long cloud emerges, only to disappear again. The wispy formation appears near the volcano Arsia Mons and gradually elongates until it reaches over 1,000 miles—about the distance from New York to Kansas City as the crow flies—before dissipating. This cycle then repeats for several months. Since it was first recorded by a probe in 2018, scientists have been unable to find a plausible explanation for the existence of this cloud, often referred to as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). Until now. Recently, researchers successfully modeled the cloud’s formation for the first time, their results suggesting that it may be driven by a physical process that has never been directly observed in any planet's atmosphere. "We found that we needed to include some exotic physics… physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before," Jorge Hernández-Bernal, a planetary scientist at Paris’ Sorbonne Université and lead author of the study, said in a press release . "Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.” Read full article Comments

title: Ice sheet expansion may have started 2,000 years ago, but we canceled that
abstract: Barnes Ice Cap sits on the central plateau of Baffin Island, in the Canadian Arctic. It is the last surviving fragment of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, which at its peak buried most of Canada under two miles of ice and locked away around 80 meters of sea level. That remnant has now yielded direct physical evidence that ice sheets might have reversed their retreat and started to grow again thousands of years ago. In a recent Science study, researchers show that the Laurentide reached its smallest size about 3,600 years ago, then started re-expanding roughly 2,000 years ago, which the team interprets as the opening move of the next glaciation. Apparently, this brand-new ice age was on its way until about 1960, when human-caused climate warming reversed it. Frozen to the bed “Barnes is the last remaining piece of one of the domes of the Laurentide Ice Sheet,” says Nicolás Young, a geologist at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and lead author of the study. As that enormous dome thinned through the Holocene, its margin withdrew up onto Baffin Island, and what's left today is the deflated core of something that was once two miles thick. The reason Barnes can testify about its own history, Young explains, comes down to the temperature at its base. Read full article Comments

title: Updated Google privacy policy says your Gmail might be used for advertising
abstract: Using Google's products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world's largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. title: Spotify ramps up policy enforcement on family plans
abstract: As reported by Music Business Worldwide , Spotify appears to be stepping up enforcement of existing policies regarding Family and Duo subscription plans by requiring users to scan a QR code in person on the plan manager's device in order to maintain access to it. Those who fail to scan the address verification QR code within seven days will see their account demoted to the free tier and be barred from joining any other Duo or Family plan for 12 months. Spotify's QR code plan enforcement. Credit: Spotify Spotify's support documentation verifies the policy after users on Reddit began posting reports of receiving the QR prompt. The enforcement stems from Spotify's requirement that family plan members reside at the same address—a seemingly reasonable policy in concept. But what if you have a child away in college, a spouse who works on the road, or any number of other circumstances that might see families separated by physical distance? Goldman Sachs analysts, in their October 15 Music in the Air: 10 Years On report, made available by HITS Daily Double , estimate that "a meaningful share of family plan users are not actual household members, but rather friends sharing a plan to reduce costs." title: Crows can evaluate visual info twice as fast as mammals
abstract: Much of what we know about how a brain makes decisions comes from studying monkeys watching dots. In a task known as a random-dot-motion task, a cloud of flickering specks drifts weakly in one direction while the subject tries to determine whether—and in which direction— it’s moving. The task has shown that in the primate neocortex, neurons gather visual evidence over time, with their firing rates climbing until they cross a threshold, when the animal commits to a decision. But avian brains don’t have a neocortex, so it wasn’t obvious how they made similar decisions. “This was the big question,” said Andreas Nieder, a neurobiologist at the University of Tübingen. “How [would] a differently organized avian brain encode decisions?” Read full article Comments

title: Ukraine learns to fight without Starlink as Musk plays politics with satellites
abstract: Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service has played a pivotal role in supporting Ukraine’s successful resistance to Russia’s full-scale invasion for years. But with Starlink having become increasingly unreliable due to Musk’s political inclinations and the latest surprise disruptions to service in Ukraine, the Ukrainians and Europe as a whole are now facing urgent questions about how to move forward without it. As the world’s largest communications satellite network, Starlink can typically support high-speed Internet and data streams for any user or vehicle equipped with a relatively compact Starlink terminal. title: 머릿속에 있던 로그 정의 기준을 모두의 AI 스킬로 만들기
abstract: 토스 앱에서 사용자가 어떤 화면을 보고 무엇을 눌렀는지는 앱로그로 남아요. 토스는 이렇게 쌓이는 로그를 서비스 품질을 높이는 목적으로 사용해요. 그래서 로그를 처음부터 정확하고 일관되게 정의해야 분석 결과도 믿을 수 있어요. 이를 위해 로그를 전담해 설계하고 관리하는 DataOps Manager와 로그 명세를 한곳에서 관리하는 플랫폼인 로그센터가 있어요. DataOps Manager는 앱로그의 규칙과 맥락을 지키며 담당 도메인의 로그 명세를 정의하고 관리 해요. 이번 글에서는 비개발자인 DataOps Manager들이 모여 로그센터에서 수동으로 진행하던 로그 정의 업무를 AI 스킬로 개선한 과정 을 소개하려고 해요. 1. 로그 정의할 때 중요한 것들 앱 화면은 끊임없이 새로 생기고 바뀌어요. 그때마다 DataOps Manager(DOM)는 사용자의 행동을 어떤 로그로 기록할지, 그 로그에 어떤 파라미터를 함께 남길지 새로 정해야 해요. 로그를 정의할 때에는 다음 네 가지를 챙겨야 해요. 로그를 정의할 때에는 로그를 정해진 형식에 따라서, 도메인 안의 맥락을 이어서, 분석에 필요한 것만 남기면서, 정책과 안전을 지켜서 정의해야 해요. 로그 규칙은 '앱로그 백과사전'에 정리되어 있었어요. 하지만 로그를 정의할 때는 규칙뿐 아니라 도메인의 맥락과 히스토리도 중요해요. 기존 로그 명세를 직접 검색해 참고할 수는 있었지만, 도메인의 맥락은 담당 DOM의 머릿속에 남아 있는 경우가 많았어요. 그래서 각자가 가진 맥락과 경험에 의존해 로그센터에서 수동으로 로그를 정의하고 관리했어요. 한 사람이 정확하게 정의하기도, 모두가 일관되게 정의하기도 어려웠던 부분을 저희는 AI 스킬로 로그를 정의하는 방식과 과정 모두를 개선 하고자 했어요. 2. 로그 정의 과정을 AI 스킬로 옮기기 로그를 정의할 때마다 앞에서 본 네 가지 규칙을 찾아보고 도메인의 맥락까지 기억하는 건 쉽지 않은 일이었어요. 그래서 한 DOM이 자신이 알고 있던 규칙과 경험을 살려, 로그 정의를 돕는 작은 스킬을 만들어 쓰기 시작했어요. 하지만 이 스킬은 만든 사람의 도메인과 경험에 묶여 있어서, 만든 사람은 편했지만 다른 사람이나 다른 도메인에서는 그대로 쓰기 어려웠어요. 그래서 저희는 이 스킬을 누가 어떤 도메인에서 작업하든 함께 쓸 수 있도록 제대로 풀어보기로 했어요. 로그를 정의할 때 거치는 판단과 순서를 개인의 머릿속이 아니라 스킬 안에 담으면, 매번 규칙을 외우지 않아도 되고 모든 도메인에서 같은 기준으로 정의할 수 있으니까요. 그렇게 만든 '로그 정의 스킬'은 로그 명세를 대신 찍어내는 생성기는 아니에요. 새 로그를 만들기 전에 '앱로그 백과사전'의 표준을 확인하고 도메인의 기존 로그 명세를 끝까지 조회해 재사용할 수 있는지 먼저 살피고 , 실제 반영은 사람이 확정한 뒤에만 실행해요. (이 스킬은 사용자의 로그를 읽거나 처리하지 않아요.) 화면 하나의 로그를 정의해달라고 하면 로그 정의 스킬은 다음의 순서로 움직여요. 스킬은 화면 디자인을 살펴보고, 적절한 로그 명세 규칙을 확인한 뒤 재사용할 수 있는 부분을 검토해 로그 명세를 제안해요. DOM이 제안된 명세를 검토해 최종 확정하면, 스킬이 이를 시스템에 반영해요. 이 과정에서 스킬, 로그센터의 CLI(Command Line Interface)인 lctl , 로그센터는 역할을 나눠 맡아요. 스킬은 맥락에 따른 판단을 안내하고, 확신할 수 없는 부분은 사람에게 물어요. 로그 이름 형식처럼 기계가 판정할 수 있는 규칙은 lctl 이 저장 전에 검사하고, 로그센터는 규칙에 맞지 않는 명세의 발행을 거절해요. 형식 규칙은 스킬에 적어두지 않고 실행할 때마다 lctl 에 묻기 때문에, 규칙이 바뀌어도 스킬은 늘 최신 기준을 따를 수 있어요. 로그 정의 스킬이 판단하고 조율하면, 로그센터 CLI가 저장 전에 미리 걸러내고, 로그센터가 저장하며 최종 판정해요. 3. 개인 도구에서 팀 표준으로 로그 정의 스킬을 함께 쓰려니 개인이 사용할 때보다 고려해야 할 게 많았어요. 한 사람의 업무에 맞춰져 있던 안내를 여러 DOM이 활용할 수 있도록 다듬고, 이후에 보완한 내용도 함께 관리할 방법이 필요했죠. 마침 로그센터와 lctl 을 개발 및 관리하는 로그 프로덕트팀에서 스킬을 lctl 에 포함해 함께 배포하자는 제안을 해주셨어요. 협업 과정에서는 문서 구조도 개선했어요. 처음엔 한 문서에 규칙과 절차를 다 담았는데, 길어질수록 AI가 중요한 규칙을 놓쳤거든요. 로그 프로덕트팀의 프론트엔드(FE, Frontend) 개발자분께 기술 검토를 받아, 한 문서에 모여 있던 규칙과 절차를 작업별로 나누고, 스킬에는 각 문서를 찾아가는 안내를 남겼어요. AI가 매번 긴 문서를 읽지 않고, 해당 작업에 필요한 내용만 찾아 읽을 수 있게 된 거예요. 이번 기회로 일하는 방식도 달라졌어요. 기존에는 업무 도구를 개선할 때, 실사용자로서 필요한 기능과 업무 맥락을 기획 과정에 전달했어요. 하지만 이번에는 그 맥락을 가장 잘 아는 저희가 AI를 활용해 필요한 도구를 직접 만들었어요. 그리고 플랫폼 조직인 로그 프로덕트팀은 저희가 만든 스킬을 검토한 후 lctl 에 통합해 배포하는 일을 맡아주셨어요. 기존에는 현업에서 문제를 발견하면 로그 프로덕트팀에 수정을 요청하고, 작업이 끝날 때까지 기다린 뒤 해결 여부를 확인했어요. 지금은 현업에서 발굴한 개선점을 DOM이 AI 스킬로 직접 개발하고, 로그 프로덕트팀과 협업해 로그센터 CLI에 통합 배포했어요. 업무를 아는 사람이 직접 만든 해결 방법에 플랫폼 조직의 기술과 운영 경험이 더해지면서, 동료들도 함께 쓰는 도구로 발전시킬 수 있었어요. 4. 더 수월하게, 더 일관되게 로그 정의하기 스킬을 함께 쓰기 시작하면서, DOM이 로그를 정의하는 과정과 시간을 쓰는 곳도 달라졌어요. 예전에는 디자인이 나오면 DOM이 화면을 보며 필요한 로그를 설계했어요. 기존 로그 명세를 재사용할 수 있는지 찾아보고, 새로 만들어야 한다면 이름과 구조를 정했죠. 스크린샷을 준비하고, 정리한 명세를 로그센터에 하나씩 입력하는 일도 직접 했어요. 지금은 디자인과 필요한 맥락을 전달하면 스킬이 기존 로그 명세와 파라미터를 조회하고, 재사용 후보와 새로운 명세를 제안해요. DOM이 검토해 확정하면 lctl 로 로그센터에 반영하죠. 기존에는 DOM이 디자인 확인부터 명세 수기 입력까지 각 단계를 하나씩 직접 처리했어요. 지금은 DOM이 화면과 맥락을 전달하면 스킬이 기존 정의를 조회해 명세 초안을 쓰고, DOM은 분석 목적과 전체 구조를 검토해 명세를 확정해요. 로그의 목적과 전체 구조에 더 집중해요. 로그를 하나씩 찾아 작성하고 옮겨 적는 일이 줄면서, 사용자 흐름 전체를 살피는 데 더 시간을 쓸 수 있게 됐어요. 스킬이 제안한 명세와 추가 정보를 바탕으로, 서비스 품질을 높이는 데 필요한 정보가 빠짐없이 정의됐는지 검토해요. 기존 로그와의 연결성을 지키기 쉬워졌어요. 예전에는 기존 정의를 직접 찾아 대조하다 보니, 이미 card_company 로 남기던 정보를 놓치고 issuer 처럼 다른 이름으로 정의할 위험이 있었어요. 지금은 스킬이 기존 로그 명세와 파라미터를 먼저 조회해 재사용 후보를 제안해요. 담당자가 의미와 사용 맥락을 확인한 뒤 재사용하면서, 같은 정보를 일관된 이름과 구조로 남기고 기존 로그와 연결해 분석하기 쉬워졌어요. 각자 챙기던 규칙과 절차를 함께 관리해요. 예전에는 로그 이름과 이벤트 타입의 규칙, 명세를 반영하는 절차를 각자 찾아보고 적용했어요. 이제는 같은 스킬을 사용해 담당자가 달라도 공통된 기준과 순서에 따라 작업할 수 있어요. 사용하면서 보완한 내용도 스킬에 반영하면 다음 작업부터 동료들이 함께 활용할 수 있고요. 로그 정의 스킬을 직접 사용한 동료들은 이렇게 이야기해주셨어요. “화면에서 새로 정의할 퍼널을 짚어 주기만 했는데 로그가 알맞게 정의돼서 정말 편했어요! 신규 파라미터나 ENUM을 지정하려면 원래 여러 단계를 차례로 거쳐야 하는데, 이제는 요청을 입력하기만 하면 바로 처리되어서 로그 정의 과정이 아주 쾌적해졌어요!” “제가 생각한 가치는 로그를 대신 만들어주는 것보다, 로그 스키마 생성 정책을
